title: Powder River Basin Mineral Rights
metaTitle: Sell Powder River Basin Mineral Rights (WY)
metaDescription: Own minerals in Campbell or Converse County? We buy Powder River Basin mineral and royalty interests, coalbed and shale alike. Get a written offer.
heroLead: The Powder River Basin sits under Campbell and Converse counties, and it's carried three different plays in forty years. Whatever formation your deed touches, we can put a number on it.
intro: Gillette is the county seat for Campbell County and the working center of the basin. Douglas anchors Converse County to the south. Between them the basin has produced coalbed methane out of the Fort Union and Wyodak coals, vertical oil out of the Muddy and Sussex, and now horizontal wells targeting the Niobrara and Turner shale in stacked laterals that run a mile or two under several sections at once.

That stacking is why an old deed can be worth revisiting. A tract that only ever produced a shallow coalbed methane well in the 1990s may now sit under a Niobrara unit two thousand feet deeper, with different operators, different royalty terms, and a different check size than what the family has seen for twenty years.

sections.heading: Coalbed Methane vs. the Deeper Shale
paragraphs: Coalbed methane wells in the basin came in fast in the late 1990s and early 2000s, produced hard for a few years, and declined steep after that. A lot of Campbell County royalty owners are still getting checks off those wells, but the checks have thinned to a trickle compared to the first few years. If that's your only production, the value in your mineral rights is mostly future, not present cash flow.

The Niobrara and Turner shale wells drilled since roughly 2010 are a different animal — longer laterals, bigger frac jobs, and royalty streams that can run strong for a decade before the steep part of the decline curve hits. If a horizontal well has been permitted or drilled on your section in the last few years, that changes what your minerals are worth even if the well isn't producing yet.

sections.heading: Who's Drilling Where
paragraphs: Chesapeake, EOG, and Devon have all held acreage and operated wells in the Powder River over the last decade, with names on the division order changing as properties trade hands. Continental Resources and Peak Resources have also been active in the Turner and Niobrara horizontal program. None of that operator history guarantees your specific section gets drilled next, but it tells you the basin is still being worked, not abandoned.

Spacing units in the horizontal program typically run a full section or larger, so one lateral well can hold interests across several separate tracts. If your mineral acres sit inside a unit with an active or recently completed well, your interest is easier to value with a real number instead of a guess, because there's a division order and check history to point to.

sections.heading: The Checkerboard Runs Through Here Too
paragraphs: Southern Campbell County and northern Converse County both carry pieces of the old Union Pacific railroad grant checkerboard, alternating sections of private and federal mineral ownership left over from the 1862 Pacific Railway Act land grants. If your section is one of the odd-numbered railroad sections, your mineral ownership is likely private and clean of federal lease terms. If it's an even section, the federal government may hold some or all of the minerals, and any well draining that section has to account for a federal lease alongside private ones.

That split matters for a buyer because federal minerals carry different royalty rates, different assignment paperwork through the BLM, and slower closing timelines than a straight private deed. We check county records and, where it applies, BLM lease status before we ever put a number in front of you, so the offer already accounts for whether your acres are checkerboard-complicated or clean private minerals.

sections.heading: What Your County Records Actually Show
paragraphs: Campbell and Converse County clerk and recorder offices hold every deed, lease, and division order affecting your tract, and that paper trail is where we start before we ever call you with a number. A deed that reserved minerals in the 1970s, a lease that's been held by production since the coalbed days, an assignment that changed operators three times — all of it shows up in the courthouse record, and all of it changes what your interest is actually worth today.

We pull that record ourselves rather than asking you to dig through a filing cabinet. If your fractional interest is small, or the chain of title has a gap, or there's an old lease still technically in force, we sort through it and explain what it means before you sign anything.

faqs.question: My minerals only ever produced from a coalbed methane well. Are they still worth anything?
faqs.answer: Often yes, but the value depends on whether the coalbed well is still paying and whether a deeper horizontal well could reach the same section. We look at both the current royalty stream and the deeper potential before we offer a number.

faqs.question: How do I find out if my section is checkerboard federal or private?
faqs.answer: The county clerk and recorder's plat records and, for federal tracts, BLM lease records show it. We pull that history as part of every offer so you don't have to track it down yourself.

faqs.question: Does it matter which operator is on my division order?
faqs.answer: It matters for how reliable and how fast the royalty payments run, and it factors into how we price the interest. A well operated by a company with a long track record in the basin values differently than a marginal or stripper operation.

faqs.question: I have Converse County minerals with no production history at all. Can you still buy them?
faqs.answer: Yes. Undeveloped acreage in an active basin still has value tied to nearby drilling activity, spacing trends, and lease bonus history in the area, even with no royalty check yet.

faqs.question: Do you buy small fractional interests, like an eighth or a sixteenth?
faqs.answer: Yes, fractional interests are common in this basin from decades of inheritance splits, and we buy them regularly. The offer reflects the fraction and the underlying acreage, not a flat minimum.
